metaTitle: Squirrel Poop: What It Looks Like (Photos)
metaDescription: Squirrel poop is dark brown pellets about 3/8 inch long with rounded ends. Real photos, squirrel vs rat and mouse poop, flying squirrels and CDC cleanup.
h1: Squirrel Poop: What Squirrel Droppings Look Like, Next to Rat and Mouse Poop
dek: Squirrel droppings are dark brown pellets about 3/8 inch long, rounded at both ends. Real photos, how to tell them from rat, mouse and bat droppings, what flying squirrels leave in attics, and CDC's cleanup steps.
excerpt: What squirrel poop looks like and how big it is, how to tell it from rat, mouse and bat droppings, why squirrels poop on porches, and CDC's rodent cleanup steps.

quickAnswer.lead: **Squirrel poop is dark brown, oblong pellets about 3/8 inch long and 1/8 inch thick, rounded at both ends: longer than a mouse's pointed 1/8 to 1/4 inch droppings, and slimmer and usually shorter than a rat's, which run about 1/2 to 1 inch.** The squirrel size comes from [Pests in the Home](https://pestsinthehome.extension.org/squirrels/how-to-get-rid-of-squirrels-in-the-attic/), a Cooperative Extension site; the rodent lengths from [Cornell IPM](https://cals.cornell.edu/integrated-pest-management/outreach-education/whats-bugging-you/rodents/mouse-and-rat-biology-and-behavior) and the rat widths from Maricopa County.
bullets: Fresh squirrel droppings are dark brown and lighten with age, Pests in the Home says; it calls them easy to confuse with rat droppings and notes that some squirrel species leave round, rabbit-like pellets.

[Maricopa County's vector control program](https://www.maricopa.gov/2141/Roof-Rat-Identification) gives roof rat droppings as 1/4 to 1/2 inch with pointed ends and Norway rat droppings as 3/4 to 1 inch with blunt ends.

Flying squirrel droppings look moist, says [ICWDM's droppings key](https://icwdm.org/identification/inspection/brown-or-black-droppings/), which shows them with urine stains directly below an attic vent the squirrels were using.

Tree squirrels are active by day, most of all in early morning and late afternoon ([UC IPM](https://ipm.ucanr.edu/home-and-landscape/tree-squirrels/)); flying squirrels are nocturnal ([UNL Extension](https://extensionpubs.unl.edu/publication/g1924/na/html/view)).

[CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/hantavirus/about/index.html) says the most common hantavirus causing hantavirus pulmonary syndrome in the US is spread by the deer mouse; its hantavirus overview does not mention squirrels.

[CDC's cleanup steps](https://www.cdc.gov/healthy-pets/rodent-control/clean-up.html): never sweep or vacuum rodent droppings; spray them with disinfectant or 1.5 cups of bleach per gallon of water, let them soak 5 minutes, then wipe them up with paper towels.

body.text: What does squirrel poop look like?

Squirrel poop looks like dark brown, oblong pellets about 3/8 inch long and 1/8 inch thick, rounded at both ends and slightly bulging in the middle. That is how [Pests in the Home](https://pestsinthehome.extension.org/squirrels/how-to-get-rid-of-squirrels-in-the-attic/), a national Cooperative Extension site, describes squirrel droppings. It adds that fresh ones are dark brown and lighten with age, and that the size varies by species.

body.alt: Eastern gray squirrel sitting up in short green grass, with gray and brown fur, a white belly and a bushy gray tail
body.caption: An eastern gray squirrel. Tree squirrels like this one are active by day, most of all in early morning and late afternoon, according to UC IPM.

body.alt: A few dark, oval droppings, some kinked or stuck together, on a pebbly concrete ledge in front of a black-and-white railing
body.caption: Fresh droppings that an eastern gray squirrel left on a concrete ledge beside a railing, by the account of the photographer, who reported seeing the squirrel leave them. Note the dark color and rounded ends; the frame has no ruler.
body.credit: (c) Andrew Sebastian, some rights reserved (CC BY), via iNaturalist

body.text: Treat that size as a rough guide: none of the other extension or agency sources behind this page gives one. [The University of Florida's guide to identifying wildlife damage](https://ask.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/UW369) says smaller oval pellets could be from squirrels, while slightly larger, smoother ovals are likely from white-tailed deer.
Is it squirrel poop or rat poop?

Start with length. [Cornell IPM](https://cals.cornell.edu/integrated-pest-management/outreach-education/whats-bugging-you/rodents/mouse-and-rat-biology-and-behavior) gives Norway rat droppings as 3/4 to 1 inch long, two to nearly three times a squirrel's 3/8 inch, and roof rat droppings as about 1/2 inch. The roof rat is the hard case, so check the ends and thickness too: [Maricopa County's vector control program](https://www.maricopa.gov/2141/Roof-Rat-Identification) describes roof rat droppings as pointed, 1/4 to 1/2 inch long and 3/16 inch thick, and Norway rat droppings as blunt and 1/4 to 3/8 inch thick. By those figures a squirrel's, about 1/8 inch thick with rounded ends, is slimmer than either, if only by about 1/16 inch next to a roof rat's.

body.alt: About a dozen dark, thick, rough-textured droppings, some with blunt ends, scattered on a white background
body.caption: Norway rat droppings photographed and identified by the New York State IPM Program at Cornell University. At 3/4 to 1 inch long, they run about twice the length of a squirrel dropping or more.
body.credit: NY State IPM Program at Cornell University from New York, USA, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

body.text: Place and timing help too. [UC IPM's Pest Notes on rats](https://ipm.ucanr.edu/home-and-landscape/rats/pest-notes/) say roof rats indoors favor attics, walls, false ceilings and cabinets, Norway rats usually stay in basements and on ground floors, and rats are mostly active at night; UC IPM's [notes on tree squirrels](https://ipm.ucanr.edu/home-and-landscape/tree-squirrels/) say squirrels are active by day.

body.needed: Gray squirrel droppings and roof rat droppings side by side on a white card beside one ruler marked in inches, each identified by a wildlife agency or extension specialist, so the two can be compared at the same scale

body.text: [The guide to rat droppings](/blog/rat-droppings) compares Norway and roof rats in detail, and if the droppings do turn out to be a rat's, [a step-by-step plan for clearing rats](/blog/how-to-get-rid-of-rats-canada) covers trapping and sealing.
Is it squirrel poop or mouse poop?

Mouse droppings are shorter and pointed. Cornell IPM gives them as 1/8 to 1/4 inch long, and [ICWDM's droppings key](https://icwdm.org/identification/inspection/brown-or-black-droppings/) describes house mouse droppings as black, hard when dry and pointed at one end, scattered in high-traffic areas. A squirrel's, at about 3/8 inch with rounded ends, is longer and blunter.

body.alt: About twenty small, dark, rice-shaped droppings, several with a pointed end, scattered across a light wooden surface
body.caption: Mouse droppings scattered on a wooden surface, in a National Park Service photograph that does not name the species. At 1/8 to 1/4 inch with a point at one end, each is shorter than a squirrel's.
body.credit: NPS Photo (U.S. National Park Service, nps.gov)

body.text: Flying squirrels are a known mix-up: [UNL Extension](https://extensionpubs.unl.edu/publication/g1924/na/html/view) says they are nocturnal and that in southeastern Nebraska their activity is often mistaken for mice, and the [US Fish and Wildlife Service's house bat manual](https://pubs.usgs.gov/rp/0143/report.pdf) says attic scratching can come from rats, mice or flying squirrels. [The mouse poop guide](/blog/mouse-poop) and [a second guide to mouse droppings](/blog/what-does-mouse-poop-look-like-canada) show them fresh and old.
What do flying squirrel droppings look like in an attic?

Flying squirrel droppings look moist, ICWDM's droppings key says, and its photo shows them with urine stains directly below an attic vent the squirrels were using. [ICWDM's guide to tree squirrel damage](https://icwdm.org/species/rodents/tree-squirrels/tree-squirrel-damage-identification/) adds that their feces mixed with urine can cause stains. Neither source gives a size.

A pile in one spot is worth noting: Pests in the Home says some squirrel species, which it does not name, keep a latrine, a dedicated toilet spot, so their droppings may not be spread across an attic like other rodents'. Flying squirrels also live in groups, in colonies of as many as 40, UNL Extension says.

body.alt: Black-and-white trail camera image of a small squirrel with a flat, furry tail climbing head-down on a brick chimney that rises out of attic insulation
body.caption: A southern flying squirrel climbing down a brick chimney inside an attic in New Jersey, caught by a trail camera. UNL Extension says flying squirrels are nocturnal.

body.text: A small hole is enough: ICWDM says flying squirrels use holes the size of a quarter, red squirrels a golf ball and fox and gray squirrels a baseball. Mice leave urine stains too; [the mouse urine guide](/blog/mouse-urine) shows theirs.

body.needed: Flying squirrel droppings and urine stains on attic insulation or a joist directly below an attic vent, beside a ruler marked in inches, from a public domain or CC0 source with an expert identification, such as a state wildlife agency or extension service

body.text: What else looks like squirrel poop?
Bat droppings, rabbit pellets and chipmunk droppings are other look-alikes.
Bat droppings

Bat droppings are smaller, and they crumble. [Nebraska Extension](https://extensionpubs.unl.edu/publication/g1667/2012/html/view) gives them as 1/8 to 1/4 inch long, black and speckled with bits of insect, and ICWDM says they pile up below the roost. The USFWS manual says they crush easily into shiny insect fragments, while small rodents' droppings are harder and more fibrous. Never test either bare-handed; see [the bat poop guide](/blog/bat-poop).
Rabbit and deer pellets

Rabbit droppings are round: UF/IFAS describes rounded, pea-sized pellets with a rough texture, and deer droppings as slightly larger, smoother ovals. Since Pests in the Home says some squirrel species leave round, rabbit-like droppings, place is the better test: ICWDM says rabbit droppings turn up where rabbits feed, and a rabbit cannot climb onto a roof or into an attic.

body.alt: A small heap of round, dark rabbit pellets in pine needles, dead leaves and grass
body.caption: Round droppings in pine litter in Alabama, identified on iNaturalist as eastern cottontail by seven users. Rabbit pellets are round and pea-sized, not oblong like a squirrel's.

body.text: Each has its own photo guide: see [rabbit poop](/blog/rabbit-poop) and [deer poop](/blog/deer-poop).
Chipmunk, insect and larger droppings

UF/IFAS groups chipmunks with rats, mice and bats as makers of small pellets the size of rice grains. Tiny black specks can point to insects: ICWDM says cockroach droppings can look like pepper sprinkled on the floor; [the cockroach droppings guide](/blog/cockroach-droppings) shows them. Droppings 2 to 3 inches long fit a raccoon, by ICWDM's figures; see [raccoon poop](/blog/raccoon-poop), [possum poop](/blog/possum-poop) and [the animal poop identification chart](/blog/animal-droppings).

body.text: Where do squirrels poop?
Look where squirrels nest, feed and travel: the attic first, then porches, decks and railings, the ground under bird feeders, and parked cars.
In the attic

Squirrels in an attic tear up insulation for nests and urinate and defecate throughout the space, Pests in the Home says. UNL Extension lists droppings, gnawed holes, shells and shredded insulation among the signs, and says tree squirrels most often get in along the gutter line or through vents. [The guide to noises in the attic at night](/blog/animals-in-attic) sorts the suspects by sound.
On the porch, deck or railing

A squirrel that poops on your porch or deck is spending time there, to feed or to pass through. UC IPM says tree squirrels travel along utility lines and fence tops and raid bird feeders, and UNL Extension says they sometimes gnaw on decks, porches and fences. The droppings in the photo above were left on a ledge beside a railing.
Under bird feeders

ICWDM says squirrels often take food from feeders meant for birds. CDC's [2002 hantavirus risk-reduction recommendations](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/rr5109a1.htm) advise against bird feeders near the home, or else a squirrel-proof feeder with spilled seed cleaned up each evening; [how squirrel-proof feeders and baffles work](/blog/best-squirrel-proof-bird-feeder-canada) has its own guide.
In or on a car

Squirrels occasionally chew the electrical wires of vehicles, notes [ICWDM's guide to preventing squirrel damage](https://icwdm.org/species/rodents/tree-squirrels/tree-squirrel-damage-prevention-and-control-methods/), so droppings under the hood are a reason to check the wiring. To clean a car, CDC says to open the hood, doors and trunk and let it air out for 20 minutes first.
Are the droppings fresh, and what does finding them mean?

Fresh droppings are usually moist and shiny; older ones tend to be dry, dull and grayish. UF/IFAS gives that rule for wildlife droppings in general, and Pests in the Home says squirrel droppings are dark brown when fresh and lighten with age. Fresh droppings in an attic mean an animal has used it recently.

Confirm it with other signs. For fox and gray squirrels, UNL Extension says property owners often hear scurrying in the ceiling shortly after dark and before dawn; flying squirrels are nocturnal, and rats mostly active at night. After cleaning up, check the same spots for a few days; new droppings mean the animals are still there.

body.needed: Fresh and old gray squirrel droppings side by side beside a ruler marked in inches, the fresh ones dark and glossy and the old ones dull and lighter, identified by a wildlife agency or extension specialist; public domain or CC0

body.text: Is squirrel poop dangerous?

Treat it with care, as you would other rodent droppings: squirrels are rodents, and CDC says rodent diseases reach people mainly when they breathe in contaminated air, which is why [its cleanup guidance](https://www.cdc.gov/healthy-pets/rodent-control/clean-up.html) says never to sweep or vacuum droppings. What CDC says about each disease:

items: **Hantavirus: squirrels are not on CDC's list.** [CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/hantavirus/about/index.html) says the most common hantavirus behind hantavirus pulmonary syndrome in the US is spread by the deer mouse, and its 2002 recommendations name the deer mouse, white-footed mouse, cotton rat and rice rat as hosts of the hantaviruses known to cause it. In [a California survey in CDC's journal](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/3/2/97-0213_article), fewer than 0.1% of the ground squirrels and chipmunks tested carried antibodies to the main US hantavirus. Mice can share an attic with squirrels; [the deer mouse guide](/blog/deer-mice) shows how to recognize one.

**Typhus from flying squirrels is rare.** [CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/typhus/about/epidemic.html) says rare US cases of sylvatic typhus occur when people are exposed to flying squirrels and their nests, and advises avoiding contact with both. A report in CDC's journal [Emerging Infectious Diseases](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/15/7/08-1305_article) says the route to people is not well understood, though the squirrels' fleas and lice become infected, and that no deaths linked to flying squirrels had been reported.

**Rabies is not a droppings risk.** CDC's [2008 rabies recommendations](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/rr5703a1.htm) say small rodents, squirrels and chipmunks among them, are rarely infected and have not been known to pass rabies to people, and that contact with an animal's feces is not a rabies exposure.

body.title: When to see a healthcare provider
body.text: If you suspect hantavirus disease, CDC says to see a physician immediately and mention the rodent exposure; symptoms of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome usually start 1 to 8 weeks after contact with an infected rodent. If you get sick after contact with flying squirrels or their nests, CDC says to see a healthcare provider and mention it.
How do you clean up squirrel droppings safely?

Soak them with disinfectant and wipe them up; never sweep or vacuum. Do it after the squirrels are out, as Pests in the Home advises. CDC's guidance covers rodents in general rather than squirrels in particular; its steps for homes and outbuildings are:

items: Open all doors and windows for 30 minutes, and leave the area while it airs out.
Put on rubber or plastic gloves.

Spray the droppings and any urine with an EPA-registered disinfectant, or a fresh mix of 1.5 cups of household bleach in 1 gallon of water, until very wet, and let it soak for 5 minutes or as the label directs.
Wipe it all up with paper towels and throw them in a covered garbage can that is emptied regularly.
Mop or sponge the area with disinfectant, including countertops, cabinets and drawers.
Wash your gloved hands with soap and water or disinfectant, remove the gloves, then wash your hands with soap and warm water.

body.text: CDC says to bag exposed insulation soiled with urine and droppings for removal. A heavy infestation, which CDC's 2002 recommendations define by piles of feces, numerous nests or dead rodents, calls for coveralls, boots or shoe covers, gloves, goggles and a respirator with HEPA filters. CDC advises avoiding flying squirrel nests, so consider having a licensed wildlife professional remove them.
What should you do once you know it is squirrels?
Get the squirrels out, close the way in, then clean up:

items: **Find the way in.** Match the hole to the animal with ICWDM's sizes, and check the gutter line and vents. UNL Extension suggests plugging a hole with newspaper: if it stays put for five days in a row in good weather, the opening is reasonably safe to close.

**Mind the young.** ICWDM says young may be present from February through August and must not be abandoned, and that one-way doors can be effective when young are not a concern. Never seal a squirrel inside: it can do a great deal of damage chewing out.
**Cut off the routes.** ICWDM says to trim limbs and trees 6 to 8 feet back from buildings, and UNL Extension calls feeding squirrels ill-advised.

**Check the rules.** ICWDM says fox and gray squirrels are game species in most states, so trapping may need a permit from your state wildlife agency; UNL notes that southern flying squirrels are fully protected in Nebraska.

body.text: [The guide to animals in the attic](/blog/animals-in-attic) covers confirming which animal is up there and sealing an attic, and [a guide to roof vent covers](/blog/best-raccoon-proof-roof-vent-covers-canada) explains which steel guards hold against raccoons and squirrels.

body.title: Photograph it, don't touch it
body.text: Photograph a few droppings beside a ruler marked in inches without touching them, and note where they lie and what time of day you hear noises. Your state's cooperative extension office or a licensed wildlife professional can use those details to help identify the animal.

faqs.question: How do I identify squirrel poop?
faqs.answer: Check size, shape, place and timing together, without touching the droppings. Pests in the Home, a Cooperative Extension site, describes squirrel droppings as dark brown pellets about 3/8 inch long and 1/8 inch thick, rounded at the ends and slightly bulging in the middle. Mouse droppings are shorter and pointed, and rat droppings are usually longer. Tree squirrels are active by day, UC IPM says, while rats are mostly active at night and flying squirrels are nocturnal.

faqs.question: How big is squirrel poop?
faqs.answer: About 3/8 inch long and 1/8 inch thick, according to Pests in the Home, a Cooperative Extension site, which notes that the size varies by species. It is the only figure among the extension and agency sources behind this page, so treat it as a rough guide. For comparison, Cornell IPM gives mouse droppings as 1/8 to 1/4 inch long, roof rat droppings as about 1/2 inch and Norway rat droppings as 3/4 to 1 inch.

faqs.question: Are squirrel droppings like mouse droppings?
faqs.answer: They are bigger and blunter. Cornell IPM gives mouse droppings as 1/8 to 1/4 inch long, and ICWDM describes house mouse droppings as black, hard when dry and pointed at one end, scattered in high-traffic areas. Squirrel droppings run about 3/8 inch with rounded ends, by Pests in the Home's estimate. Flying squirrels add to the confusion: they are active at night, and UNL Extension warns residents of southeastern Nebraska that their activity is often mistaken for mice.

faqs.question: Why is a squirrel pooping on my porch?
faqs.answer: Because it spends time there, for instance to feed or to pass through. UC IPM says tree squirrels travel along fence tops and utility lines and raid bird feeders, and UNL Extension says they sometimes gnaw on decks, porches and fences. To make a porch less inviting, CDC's 2002 advice for keeping rodents away is to avoid bird feeders near the home, or to use a squirrel-proof feeder and clean up spilled seed each evening, and UNL advises against feeding squirrels.

faqs.question: Do squirrels poop in the same spot?
faqs.answer: Some do. Pests in the Home says some squirrel species, which it does not name, keep a latrine, a dedicated spot they use again and again, so their droppings may not be spread across an attic the way other rodents' are. ICWDM's droppings key shows flying squirrel droppings and urine stains directly below an attic vent the squirrels were using, without calling it a latrine. Droppings scattered along routes fit mice better: ICWDM says house mouse droppings lie in scattered patterns in high-traffic areas.

faqs.question: Is it squirrel poop or rabbit poop?
faqs.answer: Shape usually tells you. UF/IFAS describes rabbit droppings as rounded, pea-sized pellets with a rough texture and says smaller oval pellets could be from squirrels, and Pests in the Home describes squirrel droppings as about 3/8 inch long with rounded ends. The same extension site notes that some squirrel species leave round, rabbit-like droppings, so let the place decide: ICWDM says rabbit droppings turn up where rabbits feed, and a rabbit cannot climb onto a roof or into an attic.

faqs.question: Are squirrel droppings a health hazard?
faqs.answer: Treat them with care. CDC says diseases spread from rodents to people mainly through breathing contaminated air, so clean squirrel droppings the way it advises for rodent droppings: never sweep or vacuum them, wear rubber or plastic gloves, and soak them with disinfectant or a bleach solution before wiping them up. CDC links flying squirrels and their nests to rare cases of sylvatic typhus and advises avoiding contact with them; its hantavirus overview does not mention squirrels.

faqs.question: Can you get hantavirus from squirrel poop?
faqs.answer: Squirrels are not on CDC's list of hantavirus hosts. Its hantavirus overview says the most common hantavirus behind hantavirus pulmonary syndrome in the United States is spread by the deer mouse, and its 2002 recommendations name the deer mouse, white-footed mouse, cotton rat and rice rat as the hosts. Antibodies do turn up, rarely, in the squirrel family: in a California survey published in CDC's journal, fewer than 0.1% of ground squirrels and chipmunks tested carried antibodies to the main US hantavirus. Mice can share an attic with squirrels, though, so clean all droppings with CDC's wet method.

faqs.question: Can you get rabies from squirrel poop?
faqs.answer: Droppings are not a rabies exposure. CDC's 2008 rabies recommendations say that contact with an animal's blood, urine or feces does not count as an exposure, and that small rodents, including squirrels and chipmunks, are rarely infected with rabies and have not been known to pass it to people. Clean the droppings up with gloves and disinfectant anyway, as CDC advises for all rodent droppings.

faqs.question: Is it safe to clean up squirrel droppings yourself?
faqs.answer: For a small amount, CDC gives steps a homeowner can follow: air the space out for 30 minutes, wear rubber or plastic gloves, spray the droppings with disinfectant or 1.5 cups of bleach per gallon of water until very wet, wait 5 minutes, and wipe them up with paper towels. A heavy infestation, with piles of droppings or many nests, calls for coveralls, goggles and a respirator with HEPA filters, CDC says, so consider a professional for that job.
